question: i'm new to this and just want my cloud stuff set up in code. what languages can i actually write it in? i really don't want to learn a whole new thing
reference_answer: You can define and manage cloud infrastructure using TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, and YAML. The Infrastructure as Code card on the page describes it this way: "Define and manage cloud infrastructure using TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, and YAML." It links to the Infrastructure as Code docs at /docs/iac/.

question: pulumi secrets and config across multiple environments where
reference_answer: Pulumi offers Secrets & Configuration, described as "Centralized secrets and configuration management with environments." It links to the ESC docs at /docs/esc/.

question: my database storage keeps getting close to full, at what point should I get paged vs just get a heads up?
reference_answer: Storage space remaining should be alerted at two levels: alert at 50 GB remaining as a notification, and alert at 20 GB remaining as a page. Per the three-tier strategy, the notification tier goes to Slack/email for business-hours attention, while the page tier pages the on-call engineer for immediate response.

question: self hosted api 5xx alert threshold, percentage or raw count?
reference_answer: Use the HTTP 5xx error rate as a percentage of total requests rather than the raw count. The page-level (Alert/page) tier includes a 5xx error rate > 5% as an example of a service-impacting issue that pages the on-call engineer.

question: my team wants Neo to be able to look at our datadog traces when we investigate incidents, what do I need to set up on the datadog side?
reference_answer: In Datadog, create a service account with read-only access under Organization Settings > Service Accounts. On the service account's details page, create an App Key and make sure to include the MCP read scope. Then, under Organization Settings > API Keys, create an API Key. Identify your Datadog site code (us1, us3, us5, eu1, ap1, or ap2; for example datadoghq.com is us1 and datadoghq.eu is eu1). In Neo, enter the Datadog site code, API Key, and App Key.

question: honeycomb api key scopes neo
reference_answer: In Honeycomb, go to Account > Team Settings > API Keys and select Create Management API Key, giving it a name such as "MCP Integration". Choose the Model Context Protocol and Environments scopes, then grant permissions: Read is required for all Honeycomb MCP operations (grant read for both MCP and Environments), and Write is required only for the create_board tool. Copy the Key ID and Key Secret, since you will not be able to see them again, and enter them in the corresponding fields in Neo.

question: Is the Linear key tied to me or to whoever starts the Neo task? I want to make sure comments don't show up under the wrong name.
reference_answer: Linear API keys are personal tokens. All actions Neo takes through the Linear integration are attributed to the user who created the token, regardless of who creates the Neo task. OAuth support is planned for a future release.

question: I want to turn off the jira integration just for one task so Neo doesn't touch our tickets, but leave it on for everything else. where do I do that?
reference_answer: By default, every task inherits all integrations the organization has enabled. To narrow Neo's focus for a specific task, you can toggle individual integrations off from the task composer before starting the conversation. The toggles only affect the current task; the org-level configuration is unchanged.

question: my deployment from a git push can't read stack references from another stack, why is it failing?
reference_answer: If your organization has default stack permissions set to NONE, then any deployment created by a git push or a pull request will not be able to access any Stack References, and will fail if it tries to do so. Deployments created via git push or pull request use an ephemeral stack token that has admin permissions on only the stack itself, but nothing else. To grant access, assign a Pulumi Cloud role to the deployment via Settings → Deploy → Pulumi Cloud role dropdown, or set PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN to a token with the needed permissions. A token used for stack references needs READ access to the stacks being referenced.

question: pulumi deployments env permissions NONE git push
reference_answer: If your organization has default environment permissions set to NONE, then any deployment created by a git push or a pull request will not be able to access any ESC Environments that are listed in the stack's configuration file.

question: Can I give my deployment access to ESC environments and org resources without using a static token, and what's the setup for that?
reference_answer: The recommended approach is role assignment. Open your stack's Settings → Deploy page in Pulumi Cloud, choose one of your organization's roles from the Pulumi Cloud role dropdown, then select Save. Once a role is assigned, the deployment's stack token inherits the permissions associated with that role, enabling access to stack references, environments, and organization resources as needed. Alternatively, you can set the PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable to a token with the desired permissions in the stack's deployment settings. Organization roles are managed through the Roles section.

question: my policy got added to the default group and now every deploy is failing, can I just make the default group audit instead?
reference_answer: No. default-policy-group is a preventative group containing every stack in the organization, and a policy pack added there takes effect on the next pulumi preview or pulumi up for every stack; any policy set to mandatory starts blocking deployments immediately. There is no gradual rollout, and you cannot soften the impact afterward by converting the group to an audit group. The group's type cannot be changed through the REST API, the Pulumi Cloud provider, or (per the table) the console; the default groups are fixed in identity and mutable only in membership. To stop it blocking deployments, change its policy packs: remove them, disable them with pulumi policy disable, or set their policies to advisory.

question: pulumi policy group default delete rename type change
reference_answer: The default groups cannot be deleted, renamed, or have their type changed. Delete the group: REST API DELETE rejects a default group, and the Pulumi Cloud provider has no option. Rename the group: not possible via REST API or provider. Change the group's type (for example from audit to preventative): the REST API update request has no field for it, and the provider does not support it. Because the default-policy-group cannot be deleted, renamed, or converted to an audit group, what you change to stop it from blocking deployments is its policy packs: remove them, disable them with pulumi policy disable, or set their policies to advisory.

question: I want to manage the default policy group with the PolicyGroup resource in Pulumi IaC, is that fine, or should I use something else for stacks and accounts?
reference_answer: Do not manage a default policy group with the PolicyGroup resource. That resource owns the group's lifecycle, so pulumi destroy attempts to delete it, and its policyPacks property replaces the group's entire list of policy packs. Instead, use the attachment resources to manage membership. With Pulumi IaC, each attachment resource manages a single membership, so you can declare one against a default group without taking ownership of the group itself. The provider's PolicyGroupStackAttachment resource handles stacks and PolicyGroupInsightsAccountAttachment handles cloud accounts. The provider has no resource for attaching a policy pack to an existing policy group, so policy pack membership on a default group must be managed from the console, the CLI, or the REST API.

question: Can I run my audit policy group scans on our own infrastructure instead of Pulumi's hosted runners?
reference_answer: Yes. Audit policy groups run their evaluations on Pulumi-managed runners by default. To evaluate policies inside your own infrastructure, select a customer-managed runner pool for the audit policy group. If the group has no pool set, it uses the organization default pool, and then the Pulumi hosted pool. Only audit policy groups run on a runner pool; preventative policy groups run inside pulumi preview and pulumi up wherever the CLI runs. For setup steps, see Run scans and policy evaluations on customer-managed runners in the Pulumi docs.

question: is vault actually open source or is it a different license than pulumi esc
reference_answer: Vault is not open source. It uses the Business Source License model, whereas ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed. In the summary table, ESC is listed as Apache License 2.0 and Vault as Business Source License 1.1.

question: can one env pull values from another env so i dont have to copy stuff everywhere
reference_answer: Yes. Pulumi ESC supports composability: environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated. Secret referencing: environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated from the referenced environment will automatically propagate to downstream environments. Vault has no equivalent concept; secrets are organized by path convention and maintained by hand.

question: esc env diff between versions
reference_answer: Use pulumi env diff. It shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment. Vault does not offer this comparison feature.

question: the vault cli doesnt inject secrets as env vars like pulumi env does, what do i use instead
reference_answer: The vault CLI reads and writes secrets but does not inject them as environment variables. Vault Agent's process supervisor mode covers that separately. By contrast, the Pulumi CLI, available as pulumi env, supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.

question: hey so I want to try pulumi but i have no idea what to do first, i just want to deploy something to aws. where do i even start?
reference_answer: Choose a cloud provider from the cards, such as 'Get started with Pulumi & AWS', which links to /docs/iac/get-started/aws/. Other options listed are Azure (/docs/iac/get-started/azure/), Google Cloud (/docs/iac/get-started/gcp/), and Kubernetes (/docs/iac/get-started/kubernetes/). Alternatively, under 'Or start with a coding agent', paste this prompt into your coding agent: Fetch https://www.pulumi.com/onboard.md and follow its instructions to get me started with Pulumi.

question: pulumi coding agent prompt install configure deploy
reference_answer: Under the 'Or start with a coding agent' section, paste this prompt into your coding agent of choice to install Pulumi, configure your cloud, and deploy your first stack: Fetch https://www.pulumi.com/onboard.md and follow its instructions to get me started with Pulumi.

question: how do i see the outputs of my stack but the secret ones show as [secret] or hidden, how do i get them in plaintext
reference_answer: Use the --show-secrets flag, which displays stack outputs that are marked as secret in plaintext. Example: pulumi stack get --show-secrets. The --show-secrets flag is listed under the Options section for pulumi stack get.

question: pulumi stack get json output resource ids urns
reference_answer: Use the --output flag with json for machine-readable output (pulumi stack get --output json). To include each resource's provider-assigned ID, use -i or --show-ids; to include each resource's Pulumi-assigned URN, use -u or --show-urns. Example: pulumi stack get --output json --show-ids --show-urns. The --output flag accepts default or json, and -s/--stack selects a stack other than the current one.

question: my team wants one big component that sets up the whole web app including the db and network, can i just nest the smaller components inside it?
reference_answer: Yes. Components can compose other components to build higher-level abstractions. In the example, a WebApplication component creates a Network component and a Database component inside its constructor, passing { parent: this } to each so they are nested under it. Teams can then use the high-level component without managing the individual pieces: const myApp = new WebApplication("my-web-app", { dbUsername: "admin", dbPassword: dbPassword, dbName: "myapp" });

question: pulumi component inside component parent option
reference_answer: Pass the parent option when creating the nested component. The example creates the components with { parent: this }, for example: const network = new Network(`${name}-network`, { cidrBlock: "10.0.0.0/16" }, { parent: this }); and const database = new Database(`${name}-db`, {...}, { parent: this });. The higher-level WebApplication component calls super("acme:patterns:WebApplication", name, {}, opts) before creating these nested resources.

question: the database component exposes a connectionString and securityGroupId, how do i get those out to my app in the WebApplication example?
reference_answer: The Database component declares public readonly connectionString: Output<string> and securityGroupId: Output<string>, which are set in its constructor. The connectionString is built with db.endpoint.apply(...) to produce postgresql://user:password@endpoint/dbName, and securityGroupId is set to dbSecurityGroup.id. In WebApplication, the component is stored in a variable (const database = new Database(...)), and the page says to use database.connectionString in the application configuration, for example in the ECS service, with the comment that network.vpcId and database.connectionString are used in the ecs.Service configuration.

question: where do i see the current stable pulumi version, which one is it
reference_answer: The current stable version of Pulumi is shown on the page as {{< latest-version >}}. The page text reads: "The current stable version of Pulumi is **{{< latest-version >}}**." The version number is filled in from the static/latest-version file, which is written by the CI workflow's "Update latest version" step.

question: my local copy of this versions table is out of date and I don't see the newest releases. how do I refresh the list on my machine?
reference_answer: The table body is rendered from data/versions.json, which is regenerated from pulumi/pulumi release tags by scripts/get-cli-versions.js. To refresh it locally, run `make update-versions` (requires GITHUB_TOKEN). In CI, the same script runs as part of the CLI docs workflow (.github/workflows/pulumi-cli-docs.yml), which is dispatched on each release by upstream automation. To change row layout, edit the shortcode at layouts/shortcodes/changelog-table-body.html.

question: i have a bunch of .tf files that i already run with terraform. do i have to rewrite all of them into a different language to use pulumi? that sounds like a lot of work
reference_answer: No, you don't have to convert. Pulumi's HCL runtime runs your existing .tf files directly. Set runtime: hcl in Pulumi.yaml and pulumi up deploys the configuration you already have, unchanged. Converting is optional and is only worth it if you want the infrastructure code itself in a general-purpose language.

question: pulumi convert --from hcl vs --from terraform, which one
reference_answer: Use --from terraform for a one-off translation of Terraform configuration you have been running with the Terraform or OpenTofu CLI. Use --from hcl when you have been running your .tf files under runtime: hcl and want that same program in another language. Example commands: pulumi convert --from terraform --language typescript --out ./pulumi-converted and pulumi convert --from hcl --language typescript --out ./pulumi-converted.

question: the converted output has TODO comments all over it and doesn't look like normal typescript or python code. is that expected or am i doing something wrong?
reference_answer: It is expected. pulumi convert translates HCL construct by construct and emits a TODO wherever it meets something it can't translate, so its output mirrors the shape of the HCL rather than the idioms of the target language. For most configurations, the page recommends using a coding agent instead. An agent working through the Pulumi MCP server writes idiomatic code, handles the constructs the converter can't, and can keep iterating until pulumi preview reports no changes. pulumi convert is still a fast, repeatable first pass.

question: when should I actually convert my terraform code to a real programming language instead of just running it with the hcl runtime?
reference_answer: Converting HCL to Pulumi code makes sense when: you have complex logic that is more natural in a general-purpose language; you want to test infrastructure with your language's own unit-testing framework and mocking libraries; infrastructure code needs to integrate with application code; your team prefers general-purpose programming languages; or you want Pulumi-specific features like Pulumi Policies or Automation API. If you instead want to keep writing HCL and use Pulumi's engine, state management, secrets, and cloud platform, running your HCL natively is the path.

question: my plugin folder has a pulumi file for the package, what does the runtime line need to say for a typescript one
reference_answer:
Set the runtime attribute in PulumiPlugin.yaml to nodejs for a TypeScript or JavaScript plugin. Example:

runtime: nodejs

The runtime attribute is required. Valid values are nodejs (TypeScript or JavaScript), python, go, dotnet (C# or other .NET languages), and java. YAML cannot be used to author source-based component packages.

question: PulumiPlugin.yaml main field python entry point
reference_answer:
The main attribute is optional and sets the path to the plugin's entry point, relative to the manifest. It is only needed when the entry point can't be auto-detected. Most runtimes find it by convention; for Python, __main__.py at the package root is the default. Set main only when your project layout does not match the default. Example:

runtime: python
main: src/provider/__main__.py

question: we're on the free tier and something's broken, is there any way to get a real person to look at it or do we just wait in the community slack?
reference_answer: Anyone using Pulumi open source or the free tier of Pulumi Cloud can get help through community channels: the Pulumi Community Slack (https://slack.pulumi.com/), GitHub issues (/docs/support/filing-issues/) for bugs and feature requests, the documentation, and direct chat support with the AI agent Fin via the chat box in the bottom-right corner of the website, which can also reach Pulumi support agents or open support tickets. You can also contact Pulumi support directly via the support portal (/support/new/) or by emailing support@pulumi.com. Pulumi staff are active in the community Slack and on GitHub, but response times depend on availability and are not covered by an SLA. Customers on a paid support plan get a private chat channel with Pulumi support staff for their organization, with response-time commitments.

question: pulumi support paid plan open source
reference_answer: Paid support plans are available for organizations using either Pulumi Cloud or Pulumi open source. Pulumi Cloud customers can get paid support plans at all editions of Pulumi Cloud by contacting sales (/contact/?form=sales) to upgrade. Pulumi open source users: Pulumi offers paid support plans for qualified organizations using Pulumi open source without Pulumi Cloud, so contact sales (/contact/?form=sales) to discuss options.

question: my CI keeps creating stacks and now the token that runs it has access to every stack it ever made, how do I cut that back?
reference_answer: A creator grant is added automatically when a stack is created, and it is held by the machine identity the token authenticates as. Because grants are additive, the grant is not removed by roles or organization settings, so a long-lived machine token accumulates creator grants on every stack it creates. For automation that creates stacks, have the run remove the grant or transfer stack ownership to a break-glass user or team once the stack exists. To change a creator grant after the fact: Remove the grant by opening the stack, selecting the Access tab, and deleting the automatically added Stack Admin entry. Or change the owner from the stack's details page, under Access > Settings > Change owner.

question: custom roles and ABAC rules, which pulumi plan has them
reference_answer: Pulumi Cloud's configurable RBAC features (custom roles, custom permission sets, teams, and tag-based ABAC rules) are only available in the Pulumi Pro or Enterprise editions. The built-in roles (Admin, Member, and Billing Manager) and organization-wide role settings are available in all editions, including Essentials.

question: it says a team token gets the union of the team's roles, but does it also get the org default member permissions or is that separate?
reference_answer: A team token's permissions are the union of the roles assigned to its team. It is not assigned a role directly. It also inherits the organization's default Member permissions configured in Organization-wide role settings.

question: Can a permission rule ever take away access that another rule gave a user in Pulumi Cloud?
reference_answer: No. All grants are strictly additive, meaning no rule can revoke access that another rule provides. A user's effective permissions are the union of every grant that applies to them, from the broadest organizational constraints down to the most resource-specific automatic grants.

question: my agent sandbox doesn't have pulumi installed and I don't want it wasting time installing stuff, can it just run pulumi somehow?
reference_answer: Yes. Running the CLI through npx removes the install step entirely. Any pulumi command works this way, for example: npx pulumi up and npx pulumi stack output --json. For a persistent local environment you should install the CLI the usual way, but for ephemeral agent runs npx pulumi keeps the CLI reachable with nothing to set up first.

question: pulumi do read bucket by id, anything else I need to know about it?
reference_answer: pulumi do performs direct operations on cloud resources without a project, program, or state file. Commands are generated dynamically from each provider's schema, so you can create, read, update, or delete a single resource or query a cloud API without scaffolding a program. Example: pulumi do aws:s3:Bucket read my-bucket (reads a single resource by its cloud provider ID). Also, pulumi do is in research preview and the command interface may change based on feedback.

question: Can I have my agent preview a change and only apply it if it looks right, or does the CLI support that flow?
reference_answer: Yes. Every Pulumi change has a preview that shows exactly what will be created, updated, or deleted before anything happens. An agent can run pulumi preview --json, reason about the diff, and only then run pulumi up. The change can be inspected by the agent, a human, or a policy before it is confirmed and applied.

question: my deployments keep sitting there and not running, how long can they wait before they just disappear?
reference_answer: Deployments remain in the queue for a maximum of 7 days. If a deployment is not started within 7 days — for example, because deployments are paused or the workflow runner pool assigned to the stack is unavailable — it is automatically removed from the queue and marked as `skipped`.

question: pulumi deployments queue order concurrency stack vs org
reference_answer: Deployments are queued on a first-come, first-served basis, running in the order they were submitted. On a stack level, only one deployment can run at a time. On an organization level, the concurrency limit depends on your Pulumi Cloud edition (see the pricing page).

question: ok so i made a policy and set enforcementLevel but what do the different values actually do? like what happens if i pick advisory vs mandatory, my team keeps arguing about it
reference_answer: The enforcement level can be "advisory", "mandatory", "remediate", or "disabled". An "advisory" enforcement level simply prints a warning for users, a "mandatory" policy will block an update from proceeding, "remediate" fixes the violation automatically, and "disabled" disables the policy from running. The enforcement level can be set at the policy pack level (applies to all policies) or per policy (overrides the pack level). In Python the values are ADVISORY, MANDATORY, REMEDIATE, or DISABLED, using EnforcementLevel.MANDATORY, for example.

question: python policy pack virtualenv .venv not working
reference_answer:
Python policy packs use a virtual environment specified in PulumiPolicy.yaml. The default name is "venv". If you use a different name (like ".venv"), update PulumiPolicy.yaml with runtime name python and options virtualenv set to your environment name, for example:
runtime:
  name: python
  options:
      virtualenv: .venv
See the project file reference for all available settings.

question: the stack validation part, how is that different from the resource validation one I read earlier?
reference_answer: Resource validation policies run during pulumi preview or pulumi up, examining each resource before creation or update, and execute before the desired state is sent to the engine. Stack validation policies run once, at the end of the pass, against the finished resource graph, on both pulumi preview and pulumi up. Unlike resource validation, which checks each resource as it is registered, stack validation waits until every resource in the update has been processed so it can examine relationships between them and enforce stack-wide rules. A property that stays unknown until the change is applied is still unknown when a stack policy inspects it during preview. Most policies are resource validation policies, and stack validation is useful for more complex scenarios.

question: Can I test my OPA policy locally before I publish it?
reference_answer: Yes. OPA policies can be tested using the standard opa test command from the OPA CLI. Create a test file (for example s3_security_test.rego) alongside your policy, then run the tests with: $ opa test . This is the command to run in the policy directory.

question: my config value is just a json string in esc, how do i turn it into an actual object i can reference
reference_answer: Use the fn::fromJSON built-in function. It decodes a value from its JSON representation, so it can expand JSON values stored as scalar strings into complex values. Declaration: fn::fromJSON: value-to-decode, where value-to-decode is a string containing the JSON value to decode. It returns the decoded value. If the input to fn::fromJSON is a secret, all of the decoded values are also secrets.

question: esc fn::fromJSON secret input decoded values
reference_answer: If the input to fn::fromJSON is a secret, all of the decoded values are also secrets. The function decodes a JSON value stored as a string into a complex value. Declaration syntax: fn::fromJSON: value-to-decode (YAML), with value-to-decode being a string parameter containing the JSON value to decode, and it returns the decoded value.

question: how do i see what custom roles my org has in pulumi, and can i get it as json for a script
reference_answer: Run `pulumi org role list [flags]`. It displays the ID, name, description, UX purpose, and version of each role in a human-readable table by default. Pass `--output=json` for a stable, machine-readable JSON envelope containing the same fields. Use `--org string` to choose the organization (defaults to the current default organization), and `--purpose string` to filter by UX purpose: role, role_private, role_temporary, policy, or set (default "role"). The command is marked [EXPERIMENTAL].

question: Can I list the roles for a different organization than the one I'm logged into, and how do I filter to only policy roles?
reference_answer: Yes. Use the `--org string` flag to specify the organization to list roles for; if omitted it defaults to the current default organization. To filter by UX purpose, use `--purpose string` with one of: role, role_private, role_temporary, policy, or set. The default purpose is "role". For example: `pulumi org role list --org <org-name> --purpose policy`. Note that the `--org` and `--purpose` flags are listed under Options.

question: pulumi.yaml environment key compose org-shared plus team env how
reference_answer: Teams can compose with shared organizational environments by listing them under the environment key in pulumi.yaml. The example lists org-shared and backend-team, so the service inherits configuration from both: environment: - org-shared - backend-team. This lets a team keep its own autonomy while still accessing shared organizational resources.

question: so when should I NOT do one esc environment per team? my services are kind of all over the place and some need stricter security than others, is that a dealbreaker for this approach?
reference_answer: You should not use this pattern when services within a team need strict isolation from each other, when services have different compliance or security requirements, when services span multiple teams, when you need service-level access control instead of team-based permissions, or when teams are too large to effectively manage shared configuration. If your services have different compliance or security requirements or need strict isolation, that is a reason to avoid this pattern.

question: i want to install pulumi on my mac but i dont have homebrew. what other way can i get it
reference_answer: Besides Homebrew, you can use the installation script on macOS: run `curl -fsSL https://get.pulumi.com | sh`. This installs the `pulumi` CLI to `~/.pulumi/bin` and adds it to your path. When it can't add `pulumi` to your path automatically, it prompts you to add it manually. Rerun the installer script to install later updates. You can also install via MacPorts with `sudo port install pulumi`, or download the macOS binary tarball manually and move the binaries in the `pulumi` directory to a directory on your `$PATH`.

question: winget install pulumi, does it need admin rights
reference_answer: Running `winget install --exact --id Pulumi.Pulumi` runs the standalone installer (MSI), which installs Pulumi machine-wide and adds it to your path. You don't need an elevated shell, but Windows prompts you to approve the installation. If you don't have administrator rights, use the installation script instead, which installs Pulumi for your user account only.

question: Once I've installed the CLI, how do I check that it's actually working on Linux?
reference_answer: Run the `pulumi` CLI with the version command: `$ pulumi version`. This verifies that the installation is in working order.

question: the page says I can skip the Pulumi Cloud signup when installing, but then how do I pick a different backend for state? I'm on the install step now
reference_answer: You don't need a Pulumi Cloud account to install the CLI. You'll be prompted to sign in (or to pick a self-managed backend) the first time you run `pulumi login`. Self-managed state backends such as S3, Azure Blob, GCS, or local storage are available as an alternative to the default Pulumi Cloud backend.

question: i accidentally closed the page after setting up my custom git server thing and now i cant find the webhook secret anymore. is it gone forever or can i get it back somehow
reference_answer: The webhook secret is only displayed once, right after saving the integration. If you lose it, you can regenerate it from the integration detail page. However, you will then need to update your VCS server's webhook configuration with the new secret.

question: custom vcs hmac 401 unauthorized v1 signature steps
reference_answer: To sign a request: 1. Compute HMAC-SHA256(webhook_secret, raw_request_body) using the webhook secret provided during integration setup. 2. Hex-encode the result. 3. Set the header X-Generic-VCS-Signature: v1=<hex-encoded-hmac>. The v1 prefix identifies the signing algorithm version. The Troubleshooting section also notes that a 401 Unauthorized response means you should verify the signature computation, sign the raw request body with the correct webhook secret, use HMAC-SHA256, and confirm the v1= prefix is included.

question: it says the default type is git, so how do I make a mercurial one? i dont see a vcs type option in the setup form
reference_answer: Custom VCS integrations are created with a VCS type of git by default. To configure a Mercurial integration, create the integration via the Pulumi Cloud REST API with vcsType set to hg. It is not set through the UI form described in the setup steps.

question: can I make it only deploy when files in a certain folder change, like only when something under infrastructure/ is touched?
reference_answer: Yes, use path filters. Under Stack > Settings > Deploy, set a path filter with glob patterns, for example infrastructure/**, so deployments only trigger when changed files match. Path filters require the webhook payload to include the changedFiles field. If changedFiles is omitted, path filters are skipped and all pushes trigger deployments.

question: python sdk api reference link? cant find the pulumi python docs
reference_answer: The Python SDK API reference is listed under the Pulumi SDKs section as "Python ↗" with the description "API reference for the Python SDK." Its link is /docs/reference/pkg/python/pulumi/.

question: I want to write policies for my stacks in typescript, is there an sdk reference for that somewhere?
reference_answer: Yes. Under the Policy SDKs section there is a "TypeScript Policy SDK ↗" card described as "API reference for writing policies in TypeScript." It links to /docs/reference/pkg/nodejs/pulumi/policy/.

question: ok so the cloud rest api part, where do I go to actually read about it? I want to automate some stuff against pulumi cloud
reference_answer: Under the APIs & Configuration section there is a "Pulumi Cloud REST API" card described as "Programmatic access to Pulumi Cloud for automation and integrations." It links to /docs/reference/cloud-rest-api/. For calling the REST API from code, the page also lists language-specific Pulumi Cloud SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, and Java Cloud SDKs) under the Pulumi Cloud SDKs section.

question: Does Pulumi keep patching older provider versions or only the newest one? I'm on an older AWS provider and wondering if I still get security fixes.
reference_answer: Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes. For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first. The covered providers include AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault. The previous major version is the long-term support (LTS) branch, which receives High/Critical CVE security patches.

question: lts provider release new resources or new resource properties?
reference_answer: No. An LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or new resource properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes. LTS releases only include High/Critical CVE security patches for the provider's code or its direct dependencies, plus fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship those patches.

question: i want to change my pulumi username but i dont see a way to do it, where is that setting?
reference_answer: You can rename your account from your account settings in Pulumi Cloud. Renaming your account also renames your individual organization, because the two share a name. Before you rename: update anything that addresses a stack in your individual organization by its fully qualified name (CI/CD workflows, and any pulumi.StackReference pointing at those stacks), since existing references do not follow the rename; make sure no updates are in progress, as renaming is refused while one is running; and expect a few minutes during which updates are not allowed. Renaming does not affect any cloud resources you have provisioned. Renaming is unavailable to users whose accounts are managed by a SAML identity provider, whose name must be changed at the identity provider instead.

question: delete account pulumi where
reference_answer: You can delete your account from your account settings in Pulumi Cloud (https://app.pulumi.com/user/account/settings). To get there, select your user profile, then Settings, in the left navigation bar. Scroll to the bottom of the account settings page to find the Delete account button. Deleting your account removes your access to every organization you belong to and deletes your individual organization along with its stacks, but does not delete cloud resources those stacks provisioned. This is permanent and cannot be undone. Before deleting, transfer any stacks you want to keep to another organization and make sure you are not the last admin of an organization that still needs one.

question: I'm trying to get my coworker into our org but the invite says my email isn't verified. What do I need to do before I can invite members?
reference_answer: Inviting members requires a verified email address; until yours is verified, Pulumi Cloud refuses to let you invite members to an organization. If you have not received the verification email or the link has gone stale, you can send another: select your account avatar in the top right corner, navigate to Account settings, and under your email address select the option to resend the verification email.

question: Since my SAML admin set up SSO, I can't seem to add a GitHub login to my account anymore. Why does the option disappear and how do I connect the identity I need to the account I already have?
reference_answer: The controls for connecting identities are not available to every account. An account that an organization created through SAML or SCIM cannot connect additional identity providers; it is organization-managed (see Organization-managed users). Also, in self-hosted Pulumi Cloud a provider only appears if the deployment has been configured with OAuth credentials for it. For a non-organization-managed account, to connect an identity: select your account avatar in the top right corner, navigate to Account settings, and under the identity providers section, select the provider you want to connect and complete its sign-in flow. Connecting an identity does not by itself add you to organizations; an organization admin still has to invite or add you.

question: how do i turn neo off for my whole org? i dont want my team using it
reference_answer: Neo is enabled by default. To disable Neo for your organization, navigate to Settings > Neo Settings > General in the Pulumi Cloud console.

question: neo read-only mode can it still open pulumi deployments or run pulumi up?
reference_answer: Read-only mode takes your existing permissions and removes the ability to trigger writes in Pulumi Cloud: Neo can still read state, run previews, write and refactor code, and open pull requests, but it can't trigger deployments or other Pulumi Cloud write operations directly. Neo never gets more access than you have, only less.

question: neo without github connected, can it still suggest changes or do i have to do everything myself
reference_answer: Neo can still provide code change suggestions without a VCS integration, but you'll need to apply the changes and open PRs manually. A VCS integration is optional; with one connected, Neo can read your code and open pull requests. Pulumi supports GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Custom VCS.

question: where do I set which repo my stack deploys from in the console? the dropdown has github and gitlab and some others
reference_answer: In the Pulumi Cloud console, open Settings > Deploy for the stack and choose a source. The dropdown lists the version control integrations connected to your organization, for example GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps, along with Git, No code, and None. Only integrations that are installed appear, so the exact set of options depends on your organization.

question: deploy from a repo on my own self-hosted git server, no github integration. how do i do that
reference_answer: Use the Git source to deploy from any Git repository by URL, for example a self-managed Git server or a provider you have not connected as an integration. Provide the repository URL, a branch, and an optional Pulumi.yaml folder, along with the credentials a private repository requires (typically an access token or SSH key managed with Pulumi ESC).

question: i want to see everything in my aws account even stuff made by terraform or by hand, is there a way to scan it with pulumi?
reference_answer: Discovery scans your cloud accounts and discovers all infrastructure resources. Pulumi Cloud provides complete visibility and control over your cloud infrastructure, whether resources were provisioned by Pulumi, Terraform, CloudFormation, or created manually. To get started, connect your cloud accounts, which sync and monitor infrastructure resources, and Discovery will scan them.

question: enforce policy before deploy, which doc to start
reference_answer: Get started with Policy by configuring your first policy group and enforcing compliance across Pulumi stacks and discovered cloud resources, at /docs/discovery-governance/get-started/enforce-policy-as-code/. Policy as code explains how policies, policy packs, and policy groups work together. Policy groups can apply policy packs with preventative enforcement to block non-compliant deployments, or audit mode to scan all discovered resources.

question: Can I use the Context API to see what depends on a stack before I change it?
reference_answer: Yes. The Context API lets you query dependencies, ownership, stack consumers, and change impact. The Context API overview describes how graph queries help people investigate infrastructure dependencies, ownership, consumers, and change impact. For running these queries, the Query the Context API guide covers building selectors, following relationships, interpreting responses, and checking whether an answer is complete.

question: my adapter keeps getting called by random environments from other orgs that know its url. how do i make it only accept requests from my one environment? i already check the jwt signature
external provider response format json
reference_answer:
The adapter returns a JSON object that becomes available under the response key in ESC. For example, the adapter returns:

{
  "apiKey": "secret-api-key-value",
  "apiSecret": "secret-api-secret-value",
  "endpoint": "https://api.example.com"
}

In ESC this appears as customSecrets.response with those fields, so you can reference them like ${customSecrets.response.apiKey}. The entire response can be marked as secret with secret: true, which is the default.

question: the requirements list says other status codes are errors, so what status does my adapter need to send back when things work?
reference_answer: Your adapter must return HTTP 200 for successful requests. Other status codes are treated as errors. The adapter must also run on HTTPS (Pulumi ESC only makes requests to https:// URLs), accept POST requests with Content-Type: application/json, validate JWT tokens from the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, and return JSON responses with Content-Type: application/json.

question: How do I run the example adapter on my own machine? What do I need to install first and what command starts it?
reference_answer:
Install the dependencies with pip install pyjwt cryptography, set the environment variables holding your secrets, then run the adapter script:

pip install pyjwt cryptography
export MY_API_KEY="secret-value-123"
python adapter.py

The comments note that in production you should use proper HTTPS. The adapter prints "Adapter listening on port" with the configured port (8443 in the example).

question: my pulumi up just prints Previewing update and then nothing, no resources listed, what's going on? I'm on a work laptop with a proxy
reference_answer: If you have a system-wide proxy server running on your machine, it may be misconfigured. The Pulumi architecture has three different components, running as separate processes that talk to each other using a bidirectional gRPC protocol on IP address 127.0.0.1. Your proxy server should be configured NOT to proxy these local network connections. Add both 127.0.0.1 and localhost to the exclusion list of your proxy server.

question: proxy exclude localhost pulumi nothing happens
reference_answer: If you have a system-wide proxy server running on your machine, it may be misconfigured. Your proxy server should be configured NOT to proxy these local network connections. Add both 127.0.0.1 and localhost to the exclusion list of your proxy server.

question: my team keeps picking a huge db for dev and i want to block that, how do i limit which sizes each environment can use?
so if someone asks for more storage than the size allows, what happens? does it just cap it?
I want to make sure nobody can deploy an expensive database by accident across all our teams. How do I enforce the cost rules org wide with a policy?
my teammate ran tofu apply with -var region=us-west-2 and it errored out on remote, is there a way to pass variables in without the flag?
reference_answer: The -var flag is not supported for remote runs. Use TF_VAR_* environment variables through ESC, or include a .auto.tfvars file in your configuration directory. Example ESC config: values: environmentVariables: TF_VAR_region: us-west-2 TF_VAR_instance_type: t3.micro. Also, OpenTofu automatically loads .auto.tfvars files during plan and apply.

question: vcs push apply skip approval terraform stack tag
reference_answer: By default, VCS-triggered applies pause after the plan completes and wait for manual approval. The Pulumi Cloud console shows the plan output and provides Confirm and Discard buttons. To enable auto-apply (skip the approval step), set the terraform:auto-apply stack tag to true.

question: Can I switch a stack to run plans and applies on my own machine instead of Pulumi Cloud, and how do I set that with the CLI?
reference_answer: Yes. Execution mode is controlled by the terraform:execution-mode stack tag. Setting it to local means plans and applies run on your local machine and Pulumi Cloud stores state only. You can change it from the stack's Settings tab in the Pulumi Cloud console, or with the Pulumi CLI: pulumi stack tag set terraform:execution-mode local -s <org>/<project>/<stack> and to switch back: pulumi stack tag set terraform:execution-mode remote -s <org>/<project>/<stack>

question: I saved a plan with tofu plan -out=tfplan last week, it says I can apply it later, but how long before that plan stops working?
reference_answer: Saved plans expire after approximately one week. A saved plan file is a bookmark containing a run ID, and the actual plan artifact is stored in Pulumi Cloud. When you apply a bookmark, Pulumi Cloud uses the original saved plan, so the apply matches what you reviewed even if infrastructure drifted in the meantime.

question: dotnet pulumi automation api package name
reference_answer: The Pulumi Automation API SDK is the Pulumi.Automation package. The page lists it as 'Pulumi Automation API SDK (Pulumi.Automation)' and says the Automation API lets you run Pulumi programmatically from your own code. The Pulumi.Automation package provides it for .NET.

question: I want to run pulumi stuff from my own C# code instead of the CLI. Which .NET package do I need for that, and how does it relate to the Automation API?
reference_answer: Use the Pulumi.Automation package. The Automation API lets you run Pulumi programmatically from your own code, and the Pulumi.Automation package listed on the page provides it for .NET. The page lists it as Pulumi Automation API SDK (Pulumi.Automation).

question: my policy pack needs a specific library but when I run it nothing gets installed, how do I add a new dependency to a python policy pack?
reference_answer: To install a new dependency in the virtual environment, add an entry to requirements.txt, and run the following in your Policy Pack directory. On macOS or Linux: venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt. On Windows: > python -m venv venv, then > venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt.

question: python policy pack version where do i set it
reference_answer: For Python Policy Packs, the version is specified in the PulumiPolicy.yaml file, for example: version: 0.1.0. For TypeScript/JavaScript (Node.js) packs, the version is set in package.json, and for OPA packs it is set in PulumiPolicy.yaml using the same format as Python packs.

question: If I add a policy pack and some resources in my stack already break it, does the next update just fail or can I still destroy the stack?
reference_answer: For stacks, the next preview or update of the stack will fail due to the policy violation, and the stack will need to be fixed before it can be updated. A stack with out-of-compliance resources can be destroyed. For accounts, a policy violation will be added to any account resources that are out of compliance, and violations for discovered resources are informational rather than preventative since the resource state is discovered but not managed by Pulumi.

question: I'm running pulumi preview with --policy-pack locally and also my org has policies enforced in Pulumi Cloud. Do both run, and what happens if one fails?
reference_answer: Policy Packs enforced by Pulumi Cloud are always run by the Pulumi CLI. If a Policy Pack is specified locally using --policy-pack, the Pulumi CLI will run the local Policy Pack as well as the Policy Packs enforced by Pulumi Cloud. A violation by any of the Policy Packs would halt an update.

question: ok I set up the issuer, now the policy form wants an Aud and Sub. for org tokens what do i put in those exactly?
reference_answer: For organization tokens, configure the policy's audience and subject claims as follows: Aud: urn:pulumi:org:<org-name> and Sub: repo:<organization>/<repo>:*. Replace <org-name> with your Pulumi organization name and <organization>/<repo> with your GitHub organization and repository. Then select Save policies.

question: register oidc issuer github url
reference_answer: Go to Settings → Access Management → OIDC Issuers and select Register issuer. Name the issuer and set the issuer URL to https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Then submit the form. These registration steps are the same for all token types.

question: I want my github actions workflow to act as a team instead of the whole org. how do I set that up in the yaml step?
reference_answer: Use pulumi/auth-actions@v2 with organization set to your Pulumi org name, requested-token-type set to urn:pulumi:token-type:access_token:team, and scope set to team:<team-slug>. Replace org-name with your Pulumi organization name and <team-slug> with the team's slug. The yaml is: - uses: pulumi/auth-actions@v2 with: organization: org-name requested-token-type: urn:pulumi:token-type:access_token:team scope: team:<team-slug>

question: I want a github workflow to run pulumi as one specific person on my team, not as the org. what do I need to put in the scope for that?
reference_answer: For personal tokens, set Token type to Personal in the issuer policy and set Scope to user:<pulumi-username>, where <pulumi-username> is the Pulumi username of the user the token should represent. In the GitHub Actions step, use requested-token-type: urn:pulumi:token-type:access_token:personal and scope: user:<pulumi-username>, replacing org-name with your Pulumi organization name and <pulumi-username> with the Pulumi username. Personal tokens carry that user's permissions.

question: my org's neo keeps stopping mid task and says usage hit a limit, does a small overage get billed or is it a bug? like i set 1000 and it went a bit over
reference_answer: Limits are enforced at the boundary of each Neo turn, so a task already in progress finishes its current step before Neo pauses. A small overage may still be billed as a result. If you set a $1,000 limit and see final usage of $1,003, that is expected, not a billing error.

question: neo per member limit vs org limit which one wins, member has 200 but org is 150
reference_answer: A member's Neo pauses at their effective limit — the smaller of their per-member limit and the organization limit. For example, a member with a $200 per-member limit under a $150 organization limit pauses at $150, because the organization limit is smaller.

question: my deployment just errors out right away with approval required instead of waiting for someone to approve it, is that a bug? how do i get it to wait
reference_answer: It is not a bug. Pulumi Deployments does not have a native gated deployment approval step, so the deployment does not wait for approval. Without an active access grant, the deployment fails as soon as it tries to open the credential environment, reporting that approval is required. The fix is to obtain the grant first (submit an open request, get a reviewer to approve it, and apply the request so the grant is activated), then trigger the deployment within the grant's access window.

question: deployment open approval ruleset config steps
reference_answer: In the Pulumi Cloud console: 1. Navigate to the environment. 2. Open Settings → Approval Rulesets and select Create Ruleset. 3. Select Open for the Action. 4. Specify the approvers (teams, users, or permissions), the required number of approvals, and whether self-approval is allowed. 5. Enable the ruleset. Once enabled, any attempt to open the environment without an active access grant, including from a deployment, is denied. More details are in the Configuring open approvals section of the ESC approvals docs.

question: Can I gate a git-push triggered deployment with this open approval setup, or does it only work when I kick off the run myself?
reference_answer: It fits user-initiated deployments best. Git-push and pull-request deployments run under an ephemeral stack token that has no way to hold a pre-approved grant, so open approvals can't gate them directly. To gate an automated deployment, configure it with a dedicated PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN principal whose access you approve ahead of each run. User-initiated deployments (console Deploy button, REST API, or pulumi deployment run) run with the initiating user's permissions and use that user's grant, which is the scenario open-approval gating fits best.

question: ok so i got the reviewer to approve my request but the deployment still fails with no access, what step am i missing
reference_answer: Approval alone does not grant access. Once the required number of approvals is met, you must select Apply changes, which activates the access grant. Only after the request is applied is the grant active. Then trigger the deployment while the grant is active. Also note that Grant expiration is how long you have to activate the grant after approval, and Access duration is how long the grant stays valid after the environment is first opened.

question: wait so whats the difference between preventative and audit policies? which one stops bad stuff from getting deployed
reference_answer: Pulumi Policies applies enforcement in two ways. Preventative policies block non-compliant resources before deployment, during Pulumi stack updates. Audit policies continuously scan existing resources discovered through Discovery to identify violations. So preventative policies are the ones that stop non-compliant resources from being deployed.

question: default-policy-group vs default-accounts-policy-group what do they apply to
reference_answer: Your organization includes a default policy group for each type. default-policy-group is for preventative policies and applies to all stacks. default-accounts-policy-group is for audit policies and applies to all cloud accounts. These default groups automatically include new stacks and accounts as they're created, and there are limits on how you can change them.

question: ok I'm on the policy groups tab, how do I make a preventative group for my stacks? what do I click
reference_answer: To create a policy group for stacks: 1. Select Create preventative policy group. 2. Name: Enter a descriptive name for the policy group. 3. Entities: Select Choose stacks to select which stacks this group will govern. 4. Policy Packs: Select Select policy packs to choose which policy packs to enforce. 5. Configure enforcement level (Advisory or Mandatory) for each policy pack. 6. Select Save Policy Group.

question: Once a policy violation shows up, what can I actually do about it? Can I hand it off to someone or have it fixed automatically?
reference_answer: Each policy violation creates an issue that you can act on. You can assign it to team members to delegate remediation to the appropriate owner, fix the violations yourself by updating the non-compliant resources directly, or assign it to Pulumi Neo, Pulumi's AI agent, which analyzes and fixes the violation automatically.

question: need to set up mysql so esc can rotate db passwords without downtime, what users do i make and what perms do they need?
reference_answer: You need two rotated users plus a managing user. The two rotated users alternate so one is always active while the other is rotated, ensuring 100% uptime. For MySQL, create the rotated users with: CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'user1'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'initial_password'; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON yourDatabase.* TO 'user1'@'%'; and the same for 'user2'. Create the managing user, whose privileges are scoped to a minimum, with: CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'managing_user'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'manager_password'; GRANT ALTER ON yourDatabase.* TO 'managing_user'@'%'; GRANT CREATE USER ON *.* TO 'managing_user'@'%'; Replace yourDatabase with your database name and adjust privileges as needed.

question: Using postgres. For the managing user, do I just give it CREATEROLE or does it need more than that to rotate the other two users' passwords?
reference_answer: The managing user needs more than CREATEROLE. The PostgreSQL commands are: CREATE USER managing_user WITH PASSWORD 'manager_password'; ALTER USER managing_user WITH CREATEROLE; GRANT user1 TO managing_user WITH ADMIN OPTION; GRANT user2 TO managing_user WITH ADMIN OPTION; Replace manager_password with a password you choose and note down, and make sure user1 and user2 exist first as they are the rotated users.

question: i want to create a vnet and vm on azure with pulumi, which package do i even use? there's like four of them
reference_answer: For all new Azure infrastructure projects, use the Azure Native provider (@pulumi/azure-native). It is auto-generated from the Azure Resource Manager (ARM) API specifications and covers 100% of ARM resources. Use the other providers alongside it only for parts ARM does not manage, such as Entra ID identities and Azure DevOps platform configuration. Creating a VNet, VM, storage account, or AKS cluster is handled by azure-native.

question: azure-native vs azure classic vs azuread vs azuredevops which one for managing a storage account
reference_answer: Use azure-native for Azure cloud resources such as storage accounts. Azure Classic (@pulumi/azure) is built on Terraform AzureRM, covers a subset of resources, and is not recommended for new projects. Azure AD / Entra ID (@pulumi/azuread) manages identity objects like users, groups, and apps. Azure DevOps (@pulumi/azuredevops) manages projects, repos, and pipelines.

question: Can I use the azapi package for a brand new ARM resource type that azure-native doesn't have yet, or is that what it's for?
reference_answer: Yes, a scenario where azapi has historically been useful is accessing a brand-new or preview ARM resource type before Pulumi has published an updated azure-native release. However, azapi is community-maintained, published under the @ediri/ namespace, its source repository was archived in July 2025, and its README recommends using the Azure Native provider instead. In practice, because azure-native auto-generates from the ARM spec and releases regularly, this gap is rarely significant. It uses ARM type strings and JSON body definitions, for example "Microsoft.Web/serverfarms@2020-06-01".

question: I need my AKS cluster to use a service principal instead of managed identity. The example uses azuread, how do I wire the secret into the cluster config?
reference_answer: Create an Entra ID application with azuread.Application, a service principal with azuread.ServicePrincipal using clientId: app.clientId, and a password with azuread.ServicePrincipalPassword using servicePrincipalId: sp.id. Then pass the application's clientId and the password's value into the ManagedCluster's servicePrincipalProfile: { clientId: app.clientId, secret: spPassword.value }. Example: const app = new azuread.Application("aks-app", { displayName: "aks-service-principal" }); const sp = new azuread.ServicePrincipal("aks-sp", { clientId: app.clientId }); const spPassword = new azuread.ServicePrincipalPassword("aks-sp-password", { servicePrincipalId: sp.id }); and in the cluster: servicePrincipalProfile: { clientId: app.clientId, secret: spPassword.value }. The azuread provider authenticates using ARM_TENANT_ID, ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_CLIENT_SECRET or az login.

question: my component works on my laptop but how do I get it automatically pushed to our private registry when I make a release on github?
reference_answer: Create a release workflow at .github/workflows/release.yml that triggers on tag pushes. The workflow checks out the repo, authenticates with pulumi/auth-actions@v1 using organization and requested-token-type urn:pulumi:token-type:access_token:organization, determines the version, and then publishes with: pulumi package publish https://github.com/${{ github.repository }} --publisher ${{ env.PULUMI_ORG }}. The workflow is triggered any time a tag is pushed, which happens when you create a release via the GitHub web UI (Releases, then Draft a new Release). It can also be run manually.

question: github actions publish component private registry pulumi package publish
reference_answer: Use: pulumi package publish https://github.com/${{ github.repository }} --publisher ${{ env.PULUMI_ORG }} inside a run step. pulumi/actions does not support the publish subcommand, so this step is set up manually via a run step. The publish step is conditioned with if: github.event_name == 'push' so it runs on tag pushes.

question: The test workflow runs preview on the integration folder but I'm not sure how the stack gets created on each run. Where does that happen?
reference_answer: The pulumi/actions step in the test workflow sets upsert: true, which makes sure the stack gets created if it doesn't exist yet, or updated if it does. The step runs the preview command with work-dir: tests/integration and stack-name: ${{ env.PULUMI_ORG }}/static-page-integration-test/dev. The guide also explains that env.PULUMI_ORG is set earlier in the file.

question: Can I run my component's integration tests locally without GitHub Actions, and what does the Makefile do for that?
reference_answer: Yes. Run them with cd tests/integration then pulumi preview, or with make integration-test if you have the Makefile set up. The integration-test Makefile target logs in with pulumi login --local using PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE, runs pulumi install, cancels and destroys any existing stack organization/static-page-integration-test/dev, initializes and selects that stack, sets aws:region to us-west-2, runs pulumi package add ../.., runs pulumi -C tests/integration preview, then logs out with pulumi logout --local and removes tests/integration/Pulumi.dev.yaml.

question: hurried developer stack retry backoff max duration default operator
reference_answer: Use the spec.retryMaxBackoffDurationSeconds field to control the maximum backoff duration for failed updates. It defaults to one update attempt per day (86400 seconds), but you can lower it for faster retry cycles during development.

question: ok so my stack needs an env var but I dont want to put it in envRefs, can I set env vars from an init container somehow? how would that look in the yaml
reference_answer: Yes. You can set environment variables dynamically through init containers by writing to the $PULUMI_ENV file. Environment variables set this way affect the Pulumi CLI during deployment operations. For example, under spec.workspaceTemplate.spec.initContainers you can add a container that runs: sh -c with echo "PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE=my-passphrase" >> $PULUMI_ENV and echo "MY_CUSTOM_VAR=value" >> $PULUMI_ENV, using the image busybox.

question: Can I point a Stack at a Flux GitRepository source instead of giving it a projectRepo URL directly?
reference_answer: Yes. Flux sources are specified as Custom Resources in a Kubernetes cluster, such as GitRepository, OCIRepository, and Bucket resources. To refer to a Flux source object, use the spec.fluxSource field, and use spec.fluxSource.dir to refer to a program directory within the source artifact. The example assumes Flux is already installed in your cluster. In the example, spec.fluxSource.sourceRef is set with apiVersion source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1, kind GitRepository, and name set to the GitRepository's metadata.name.

question: frustrated beginner here. I want my stack settings to be a nested object like database host and port, not just plain strings. can I load that from a ConfigMap?
reference_answer: Yes. Stack configuration supports objects, arrays, numbers, and booleans, not just strings. You can reference a ConfigMap for complex configuration using the json: true flag under spec.configRefs. For example, store a JSON document under a key like database.json in a ConfigMap's data, then in the Stack spec set configRefs with database: name: app-settings, key: database.json, and json: true so it is parsed as JSON. Note that Secrets are not a supported source of structured configuration values.

question: i want my deployment to always use the same template version so nothing changes unexpectedly, how do i pin the registry url?
reference_answer: Append @{version} to the registry URL to pin to a specific semver version, for example registry://templates/pulumi/community/aws-static-website@1.0.0. Omitting the version uses the latest published version, which is resolved at the time of use. For reproducible deployments, specify an explicit version.

question: registry url format for templates, what goes where
reference_answer: The format is registry://{resource-type}/{source}/{publisher}/{name}[@{version}]. For templates, the resource-type is always templates, giving registry://templates/{source}/{publisher}/{name}[@{version}]. The components are: source is the registry source or namespace (e.g., pulumi), publisher is the organization that published the resource, name is the resource name, and version is optional semver (omit it for the latest version).

question: my pulumi update keeps failing with conflicts and i don't know how to recover, where do i look?
reference_answer: The page points to a Troubleshooting guide at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/, described as a way to "Diagnose and recover from common failures including update conflicts, destroy failures, and CI/CD pipeline issues." It sits under IaC Operations, which covers day-2 workflows for running Pulumi, including troubleshooting and debugging.

question: pulumi bug report which github repo
reference_answer: Use the GitHub Issues section, which links to /docs/support/filing-issues/. It explains "how to report bugs and request features in the right repository."

question: i want pulumi cloud to encrypt our stuff with a key we own in aws. where do i even start, what do i set up first?
reference_answer: Start in AWS by creating an identity provider. In the IAM console, choose Identity providers, then Add provider. Select OpenID Connect, set the Provider URL to https://api.pulumi.com/oidc, and set the Audience to the name of your Pulumi organization prefixed with aws: (for example aws:{org}). Then click Add provider. After that, assign an IAM role (Create a new role, Web identity, select api.pulumi.com/oidc as the identity provider and your Pulumi organization as the audience), review the trust policy, create the AWS KMS key, and finally add the customer managed key in Pulumi Cloud using the role ARN and key ARN.

question: trust policy json aws kms pulumi cmk condition statementequals sub
reference_answer: The trust policy for the IAM role should look like this: {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/api.pulumi.com/oidc"}, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"api.pulumi.com/oidc:aud": "aws:<pulumi-org-name>", "api.pulumi.com/oidc:sub": "pulumi:cmk:pulumi.organization.login:<pulumi-org-name>"}}}]}. Ensure the audience and subject are configured as shown, found under the trust relationships tab of the role.

question: Can I use an AWS KMS key as the customer managed key for Pulumi Cloud, and how do I register it once the role and key exist?
reference_answer: Yes. Once you have the role ARN and key ARN, go to Pulumi Cloud, navigate to Settings, then Organization, then Customer Managed Keys. Select Add Customer Managed Key, enter a unique name for the key, provide the Role ARN of the IAM role you created, and provide the Key ARN of the AWS KMS key. Alias ARNs are also supported. To set the key as your organization's default, or to disable a key later, see the Customer managed keys concept page. Note that when you add your first customer managed key, all data keys encrypted with the Pulumi-managed key are automatically re-encrypted with the new key, but the encrypted data itself does not change.

question: i use claude code, how do i get the pulumi skills installed? what commands
reference_answer: For Claude Code users, the plugin system provides the simplest installation. Run these commands: /plugin marketplace add pulumi/agent-skills, then /plugin install pulumi (all end-user skills: authoring, migration, and Neo handoff). If you prefer a subset, install pulumi-migration (Migration skills only), pulumi-delegation (Neo handoff skill only), or pulumi-package-maintenance (provider-repo maintenance skills, for provider authors) instead of pulumi, not alongside it, since pulumi already includes both migration and delegation.

question: Do I need to install anything to use these skills if I'm already using Neo? I just want my Pulumi stuff to work.
reference_answer: No. Neo ships with the Pulumi Agent Skills catalog built in. You don't need to install or configure anything, and the catalog updates with each Neo release. Neo discovers each skill's SKILL.md and loads relevant skills automatically when a task calls for them, so you never need to name a skill yourself.

question: Can I use the universal installer to add just the migration skills to Junie, or do I have to install everything?
reference_answer: You can install each end-user skill group separately with the universal installer. The migration group is installed with: npx skills add pulumi/agent-skills/migration --skill '*' (5 migration skills). To install a group for a specific agent such as Junie, use the --agent flag, for example: npx skills add pulumi/agent-skills/pulumi --skill '*' --agent junie. The example shown uses the pulumi group; the same --agent flag can be used with the other groups.

question: it says to install pulumi and pulumi-migration both is fine right? or will the skills duplicate
reference_answer: Not both. The pulumi plugin already bundles the Pulumi, Migration, and Delegation skill groups together in a single install. Installing pulumi-migration or pulumi-delegation alongside pulumi would install the same skills twice. Install pulumi-migration or pulumi-delegation on their own only if you need a subset, rather than alongside pulumi. The pulumi-package-maintenance plugin, however, combines fine with any of the others.

question: hurried developer: install gh cli deployment pre-run command vs custom image, which one
reference_answer: Pre-run commands are best for one-off tools, scripts, or quick experiments. The install runs on every deployment, adding setup time to each run. A custom executor image is best for stable tool sets used on every deployment, but it means slower cold starts on fresh runners and an image you have to maintain. Pre-run commands need no image to build or maintain, are easy to change, and work with the default pulumi/pulumi image so cold starts stay fast. Reach for a custom image only when the install cost starts to hurt. For example, a pre-run command such as `apt-get update && apt-get install -y my-tool` installs the tool on every run.

question: I'm trying to use a private ECR image for my deployment executor and it keeps failing after a while even though it worked at first. what's going on? do I need to use IAM instead of pasting the password?
reference_answer: Custom executor images in a private registry require static username and password credentials in the deployment settings. OIDC and IAM-role-based pulls are not supported for custom executor images. This rules out a private Amazon ECR registry, because its registry password is an authorization token from `aws ecr get-login-password` that expires after 12 hours, so a pasted token soon stops working and deployments can no longer pull the image. A public image on Amazon ECR Public needs no credentials and works fine. If you need short-lived registry credentials or need to pull a private image from ECR, Customer-managed runners run in your own infrastructure and can use whatever pull mechanism you configure, including an IAM role.

question: I just need python for my pulumi program in a custom image, which base image should I use so it's not huge?
reference_answer: Pick the smallest base that has the language runtime you need, since pull time scales with image size. Use the single-language variant `pulumi/pulumi-python` (200–400 MB), which contains the pulumi CLI plus one language runtime, and is intended for single-language projects. If you will install your own language runtime, or use a single language version not in the SDK images, use `pulumi/pulumi-base` (~200 MB), which contains only the pulumi CLI. Avoid the full `pulumi/pulumi` image (~2 GB) unless you are working on a polyglot project, because it copies roughly 2 GB of layers your project will not use.

question: Can I use an alpine based image as my custom executor image to keep it small?
reference_answer: No. A custom executor image must be a Linux image, include `curl` on `$PATH`, include the `pulumi` CLI on `$PATH`, include the language runtime(s) for the projects that will use it, and use a glibc-based libc. Most Pulumi resource provider plugins are glibc-linked, so musl-only images such as Alpine are not supported. If you start from one of the `pulumi/*` base images, all of these requirements are already true.

question: my stack is a python project but my policy pack is typescript, do i need to install python on the machine running pulumi for the policies to run?
reference_answer: No, the pack's runtime determines what is required, not the language of your Pulumi program. A policy pack's runtime is declared in PulumiPolicy.yaml. A Python or Go stack governed by a TypeScript policy pack still needs Node.js, because the pack declares runtime: nodejs. So for a TypeScript pack you need Node.js installed on the machine running Pulumi, regardless of the stack's language.

question: policy pack node.js bun
reference_answer: Bun cannot substitute for Node.js. Although Pulumi supports runtime: bun for Pulumi programs, a policy pack that declares runtime: nodejs is always executed with Node.js, even when the stack's own program uses Bun. Node.js must be installed on the machine running Pulumi.

question: I want my CIS compliance policies to block deployments in prod but only warn in dev. Is there a way to do that without copying the pack twice?
reference_answer: Yes. Enforcement is set per policy: a policy can warn (advisory), block the deployment (mandatory), fix the violation automatically (remediate), or be turned off (disabled). A policy group can override these levels for the packs it applies, so the same pack can warn in one group and block in another. Also, a policy can define a configuration schema that turns fixed values into parameters set when the pack is applied, letting one pack enforce a stricter threshold in production than in development without maintaining two copies.

question: we pinned our policy group to v1.2.0 and I published v1.3.0 with pulumi policy publish. did enforcement just change for everyone? how do i get the new version picked up?
reference_answer: No. Publishing creates a new version rather than replacing the existing one, and a policy group references a particular version, so publishing does not change what is enforced until a group is pointed at the new version. To track releases automatically instead, enable latest rather than a specific version. Publish with the pulumi policy publish command, which creates a new version.

question: i want my pulumi environment to pull our api keys out of google's secret manager instead of me pasting them in by hand. what do i put in the yaml? i keep getting lost on the login part
reference_answer:
Use the gcp-secrets provider, which dynamically imports Secrets from Google Cloud Secrets Manager into your Environment and returns a map of names to Secrets. Log in first with the gcp-login provider, then pass that login into gcp-secrets and list the secrets to access. Example:

values:
  gcp:
    login:
      fn::open::gcp-login:
        project: 123456789
        oidc:
          workloadPoolId: pulumi-esc
          providerId: pulumi-esc
          serviceAccount: pulumi-esc@foo-bar-123456.iam.gserviceaccount.com
    secrets:
      fn::open::gcp-secrets:
        login: ${gcp.login}
        access:
          api-key:
            name: api-key
          app-secret:
            name: app-secret
  pulumiConfig:
    apiKey: ${gcp.secrets.api-key}
    appSecret: ${gcp.secrets.app-secret}

Each key under access is a local name, and its name field is the Google Cloud secret name. You then reference the values as ${gcp.secrets.<name>}.

question: esc gcp oidc how to verify setup pulumi env open
my pulumi up got killed halfway and now it says pending operations, how do i get my stack back to normal
reference_answer: If the Pulumi CLI is interrupted during a deployment, the next update shows a warning about pending operations. First cancel the update with `pulumi cancel`. If that fails with `error: [400] Bad Request: the update has already completed`, you can safely ignore it. Then run `pulumi refresh` to remove pending operations cleanly.
